newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec's Bouchard says no snap election.
newsitem.headline: Quebec's Bouchard says no snap election.

text.p: Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard said on Tuesday he would not call a snap election in the mainly French-speaking Canadian province despite rumours he may do so in the coming months.

"My intention this morning is not to shuffle my cabinet (but) to keep a winning team around us and not to call an election," Bouchard told reporters in Quebec City. "I think that we have the trust of the population. The population wants us to govern and we will govern."
His comments came after a turbulent weekend convention of his ruling separatist Parti Quebecois at which party members supported his leadership by a lower-than-expected margin.

Bouchard left the convention with his wife Audrey to reflect on his political future, raising speculation that he might resign. But he told reporters on Tuesday he had not seriously considered stepping down.
"I never thought about resigning," he said. "I had to reflect with my family."

Bouchard, a mecurial, iron-fisted political leader, was criticised by Quebec newspapers after the convention for hinting that he might resign and creating a drama around himself and his position as leader. Quebec City's Le Soleil commentator Michel David wrote in a column on Monday: "There is no doubt he comes away from the convention weakened."
Bouchard rejected the press criticism. "I did not lose my cool," he said. "I am as cold as ice."
Quebec separatists, who still have three years left of their current mandate, lost a referendum on the separation of Quebec from Canada by a thin-razor margin on Oct. 30, 1995.
